signatures.member: private static JsonObject serializeSetting(Setting<?> setting) — instanceof chain: BooleanSetting->"boolean" | NumberSetting->"number" | MultiChoiceSetting->"multi_choice" | ModeSetting->"mode" | ColorSetting->"color" | StringSetting->"string" | else -> return null

signatures.member: private void applyBind(Module module, long now)
signatures.notes: THE ONLY consumer of BindMode. Body: `if (!bind.isBound() || bind.getMode() == BindMode.TOGGLE) return;` -> so ONLY HOLD is implemented. Then satisfied = bind.matches(pressedKeys); if satisfied: clear holdReleaseAt, stamp holdSatisfiedAt if absent, and `if (!module.isToggled() && now - since >= bind.getEnableDelayMs()) module.setToggled(true)`. else if (module.isToggled() && holdSatisfiedAt.containsKey(module)): remove holdSatisfiedAt, holdReleaseAt.putIfAbsent(module, now). Finally: if holdReleaseAt has an entry and now - releasedAt >= bind.getDisableDelayMs(), remove it and setToggled(false). Called from onRawKey(int,int) (every GLFW press/release of any key, over ALL modules) and from tickHolds() via public tick() (every ClientTickStartEvent, over ALL modules).

gotchas: BindMode.TOGGLE IS DEAD CODE. applyBind's first line is `if (!bind.isBound() || bind.getMode() == BindMode.TOGGLE) return;` and I grepped all of src/ for getBind()/getKeybind()/isBound()/BindMode. - the only other consumers are ProfileSnapshotCodec (serialization), BindModal (the ClickGUI editor UI) and DetailPane (a badge label). NOTHING maps a pressed key to module.toggle() for TOGGLE mode. Since ModuleBind.NONE defaults to BindMode.TOGGLE, a bind set through the modal with the default mode does nothing at all in-game. The only working toggle paths are HOLD binds and the ClickGUI (Enter on selection, right-click a module row, DetailPane click).

Module.onKeyPress does NOT fire while the module is disabled. Both onKeyPress and onMouse are dispatched through forEachToggledBoolean(...), which iterates the cached `toggledModules` list (rebuilt by refreshToggledModules() from modules.stream().filter(Module::isToggled)). A module therefore CANNOT implement its own hold-key from inside onKeyPress - it would never see the press that should turn it on. Do it by subscribing to KeyInputEvent directly (the established pattern: Sprint, MovementFix, SprintReset and CPSDisplayElement all call MicaEvents.subscribe(...) in their own constructor and self-gate on isToggled()).

Asymmetric edge visibility for HOLD-bound modules inside onKeyPress: the KeyInputEvent listener runs onRawKey(...) (which can setToggled(true), and setToggled synchronously refreshes toggledModules in its finally block) BEFORE the onKeyPress fan-out. So with enableDelayMs == 0 a hold-bound module DOES receive the press that enabled it - but on release onRawKey disables it first, so it NEVER receives the matching release. Any state machine built on onKeyPress edges will get stuck.

A module returning false from onKeyPress silently disables the whole ClickGUI key router for that key. The line is `if (veto || ClickGUI.consumeKey(e.key(), e.action())) e.cancel();` - Java's || short-circuits, so on veto consumeKey is never called: no GUI open/close key, no ESC handling, no bind-modal capture, no text-field editing for that keystroke.

Packet and outline vetoes are aggregate and global, not per-module. forEachToggledBoolean runs EVERY toggled module (no short-circuit) and cancels if ANY returned false - so one module vetoing a packet cancels it for the whole client, and other modules' hooks still ran and saw it.

Any Setting subclass that is not one of BooleanSetting, NumberSetting, MultiChoiceSetting, ModeSetting, ColorSetting, StringSetting silently fails to save - ProfileSnapshotCodec.serializeSetting's instanceof chain ends in `else { return null; }` and the null is dropped by the caller with no log. ActionSetting/DescriptionSetting/HyperlinkSetting are intentional; a NEW custom subclass hits the same branch. Extending one of the 6 (e.g. `class MySetting extends BooleanSetting`) does persist, because instanceof matches.

ProfileSnapshotCodec.apply() calls module.setToggled(...) BEFORE it applies the settings array, so a module's onEnable() runs against DEFAULT setting values during config load. Same for onLoad(), which bootstrap() calls before ConfigManager.autoLoad(). Read settings lazily (in onPreUpdate / at use time), never cache them in onEnable or onLoad.

Settings are keyed by display name, matched case-insensitively via Module.getSetting -> equalsIgnoreCase. Renaming a setting's display name silently orphans every saved value (deserializeSetting just `return`s when getSetting is null). Two settings with names differing only in case collide - the first in the list wins.

Silent value coercion on load, per type: ModeSetting.setValue IGNORES any value not in its modes list (rename a mode option -> saved value dropped, setting stays at default); MultiChoiceSetting filters out selections no longer in options; NumberSetting clamps to [min,max] and rounds when integerOnly; StringSetting truncates to maxLength. None of these log anything.

HOLD enable-delay leak: in applyBind the cleanup branch is `else if (module.isToggled() && holdSatisfiedAt.containsKey(module))`. If you release the key BEFORE enableDelayMs elapses, the module is not toggled, so that branch is skipped and holdSatisfiedAt keeps the stale timestamp. The next press reuses the old `since`, making `now - since >= enableDelayMs` instantly true - the enable delay is bypassed on every press after the first aborted one.

Binds are keyboard-only. pressedKeys is fed exclusively from onRawKey, which is called only from the KeyInputEvent listener; MouseButtonEvent never touches it, and GLFW_REPEAT returns before any bind work. pressedKeys is also never cleared on focus loss, world change, or GUI open, so a key released while the game window is unfocused stays 'held' and a HOLD bind can latch on.

NotificationManager.update(float) is called ONLY from NotificationsModule.updateDimensions (invoked from its render()). If the "Notifications" HUD module is disabled, posted toasts never age out and never render - the deque just fills to HARD_CAP = 32 and old entries get trimmed. Posting is silently invisible, with no error. Also note post()'s maxVisible loop calls removeFirst / dismiss / addFirst / break, so it never actually shrinks the deque; it only marks the oldest for removal and relies on update() to drop it.

Duplicate suppression in NotificationManager.post compares only against peekLast() within duplicateCooldownMs (350 ms default), and lastDuplicateAt is stamped on EVERY accepted post. Two alternating toasts posted rapidly both get through; the same toast twice in 350 ms gets the second one dropped silently.

PacketPostSendEvent and PacketPostReceiveEvent are subscribed by ModuleManager with empty lambdas - there is no Module hook for them. If you need post-send/post-receive, subscribe to MicaEvents yourself.

ModuleManager registers two separate ClientTickStartEvent listeners, both at NORMAL, and ordering depends on registration sequence (ListenerList sorts by -priority then sequence): the constructor's wireEventDispatchers() one (onPreGameTick -> onPreUpdate -> processRotations) is registered first, then bootstrap()'s `e -> tick()` (hold-bind delay resolution). So hold-bind enable/disable from a *delay* lands AFTER that tick's onPreUpdate. RotationDiagnostics, when enabled, subscribes ClientTickStartEvent at HIGHEST and therefore runs before both.

ModuleManager throws away every Subscription that subscribe() returns, so its dispatch can never be unwired; the manager is a synchronized lazy singleton for the process lifetime. If YOUR module subscribes in its constructor (the house pattern), keep the Subscription only if you actually intend to unsubscribe - otherwise self-gate on isToggled() inside the handler like Sprint does.

Module.onDisconnect is the ONE hook that is not gated on isToggled() (forEachAll), and ConfigManager.autoSave() runs right after it - so state you mutate in onDisconnect is what gets persisted. onWorldJoin, by contrast, is gated.

No chat / item / block-placement helper exists anywhere under dev/technix/client - you must call Minecraft classes directly. Watch the client-vs-server split: to print a message locally use LocalPlayer.sendSystemMessage(Component) (verified to route to minecraft.gui.chatListener().handleSystemMessage(message, true)); ClientPacketListener.sendChat/sendCommand talk to the SERVER and re-enter this project's ChatSendEvent via ClientPacketListenerMixin. There is no ServerLevel/ServerPlayer path available from here at all.
